PR5-F-01.hint: Set each factor equal to zero. A quadratic factor with no real zeros gives complex zeros: solve it with the square root property or the quadratic formula and use \(i=\sqrt{-1}\). Each zero \(r\) gives a linear factor \((x-r)\).
slips: Dropping the \(\pm\) when you take a square root of a negative number. Complex zeros come in pairs.
Writing the factor as \((x+r)\) when the zero is \(r\). The factor is \((x-r)\).
Leaving out a repeated factor when you write the product of linear factors.

PR5-F-02.hint: Use the quadratic formula (or complete the square) on the quadratic factor and keep the answer exact. Each zero \(r\) gives a linear factor \((x-r)\).
slips: Rounding a radical to a decimal when the question asks for exact values.
Getting the sign wrong in a factor. If the zero is \(2+\sqrt{3}\), the factor is \(x-2-\sqrt{3}\).

PR5-A-01.hint: Divide by the factor that the given zero provides. The quotient is a quadratic you can solve with the quadratic formula.
slips: Dividing by \(x+r\) when \(r\) is the zero. A zero \(r\) gives the divisor \(x-r\).
Stopping after the division and never writing the linear factors for the zeros of the quotient.
